opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more interesting shifts of the last few years, because if you went back to around 2016 or 2018, a lot of us in robotics were really excited about off-policy methods. The dream was you'd have this giant replay buffer, all the data you've ever collected, and you'd squeeze value out of every transition with Q-learning. That's very appealing when data is expensive, like when you have physical robots breaking and needing to be reset.

But in practice, off-policy RL is just really finicky. You're bootstrapping a value function on data from a different distribution than the one your current policy visits, and the errors compound. The Q-function becomes overly optimistic about actions it's never actually seen work, the policy exploits those errors, and things fall apart. You end up spending a lot of your research effort fighting instability rather than making progress.

On-policy methods are, in a sense, dumber, but they're honest. The gradient you compute is about the policy you actually have, on the states it actually reaches. You don't have to trust a learned critic to extrapolate correctly. And once compute and simulation, or in the LLM case, sampling, got cheap enough, the sample-efficiency argument for off-policy methods mostly evaporated. If you can generate fresh rollouts, stability beats efficiency.

So where did the off-policy data go? It didn't disappear. It moved upstream. Instead of feeding it into a Bellman backup, we use it for pretraining or imitation learning. You take all the human demonstrations, internet text, teleoperation logs, and you use them to build a really strong prior policy. Then on-policy RL is a relatively small fine-tuning step on top. Language models are the clearest example: pretraining is basically giant off-policy behavior cloning, and RL from human feedback or verifiable rewards is the on-policy refinement.

I think the deeper lesson is that supervised learning is extremely good at absorbing large, diverse, off-policy datasets, and RL is good at fixing the last mile of behavior relative to what you actually care about. Trying to get one algorithm, off-policy RL, to do both jobs at once turned out to be harder than just splitting the work.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the short answer is that off-policy learning is a promise that mostly hasn't paid off at scale, and on-policy learning is the thing that actually works when you have a big model and a lot of compute.

Let me unpack that a bit. The dream of off-policy RL was always very appealing. You have this giant pile of experience sitting on disk, maybe from humans, maybe from old versions of your policy, and you'd like to squeeze every bit of signal out of it without having to go back and collect more. Q-learning, offline RL, all of that. And in principle that's strictly better, right? Why throw away data?

The problem is that it just turns out to be really hard to get right. When you're evaluating a policy on data that policy didn't generate, you're fundamentally asking a counterfactual question: what would have happened if I'd done something different here? And answering that requires a model, implicitly or explicitly, of the parts of the state space you've never visited. Function approximators are bad at that. They extrapolate confidently and wrong, and then you bootstrap off those wrong estimates and the whole thing diverges. People have spent a decade putting bandaids on this, conservative Q-learning, behavior regularization, importance weight clipping, and every one of those is essentially saying, "please don't trust the off-policy signal too much." At some point you have to ask what you're buying.

On-policy methods sidestep the entire problem. PPO, GRPO, whatever flavor you like, they all say: generate samples from the current policy, score them, nudge the policy toward the good ones, repeat. There's no counterfactual, no distribution mismatch to correct for. It's dumb and sample inefficient, but it's stable, and stability is what you want when a training run costs millions of dollars and you can't afford to babysit it.

And the thing that changed the calculus is that sample efficiency stopped being the bottleneck. In the language model world, your environment is often just a reward model or a verifier, and generating rollouts is comparatively cheap relative to the cost of a gradient step on a huge model. So the classic argument for off-policy, that environment interaction is expensive, mostly evaporates. You'd rather spend the compute on more rollouts than on fancy machinery to reuse old ones.

Now, that doesn't mean off-policy data went away. It just got pushed upstream, into pretraining and supervised fine-tuning. That's really what imitation learning is: you're ingesting an enormous amount of off-policy experience, you're just doing it with maximum likelihood instead of a Bellman backup, which is a much better-behaved objective. So the stack that has emerged is, learn the priors from off-policy data with a stable supervised loss, then do the actual decision-making refinement on-policy where you can trust the signal. The off-policy data shapes what the policy is capable of considering, and the on-policy loop decides what it actually does.

I'd also say there's a pragmatic engineering reason. On-policy with a small trust region is a very forgiving algorithm. You can mess up the reward, you can have noisy verifiers, and you mostly just learn slowly rather than catastrophically. Off-policy methods tend to fail in dramatic and hard-to-debug ways. When you're a team trying to ship, you pick the algorithm whose failures are boring.

The thing I'd keep an eye on is whether this stays true. If generating rollouts becomes the expensive part again, say in robotics where you're constrained by real-world interaction, or in long-horizon agentic tasks where a single episode takes hours, then the pressure to reuse data comes right back, and people will have to revisit the off-policy question seriously. My guess is the answer will look less like classic Q-learning and more like better world models, so you can go on-policy inside a learned simulator. But that's speculation.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how much you trust your learning signal once the policy moves away from the data you collected. With on-policy training, you’re asking a relatively clean question: “Under the behavior I currently have, which actions worked better than expected?” The data directly answers that question.

With off-policy training, you’re trying to learn about a policy using experience generated by some other policy. That’s potentially much more efficient, but you have to correct for the mismatch somehow. Importance sampling can have enormous variance over long sequences. If you use a learned value function instead, you can get this failure mode where the policy discovers actions that the value function mistakenly thinks are great. Then you’re optimizing the errors in your predictor.

So I wouldn’t say off-policy data has stopped being useful. It’s extremely useful for learning representations, learning models of the world, or just learning a good initial policy through imitation. But those are ways of extracting knowledge from the data without fully trusting it to tell you the value of a different policy.

The pattern is something like: use all the historical data to get a strong starting point, then use fresh interaction to figure out whether your proposed improvements actually work. And when generating fresh experience is relatively cheap, that’s a pretty attractive tradeoff. In robotics, where collecting experience is expensive, there’s much more pressure to make off-policy learning work. So I think this convergence reflects both the stability of the algorithms and the economics of collecting data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to how much you can trust your value estimates. Off-policy learning is very appealing because, in principle, you should be able to reuse everything you’ve ever experienced. But you’re learning from actions taken by a different policy, and then asking, “What would happen if my current policy did something else?” That requires some generalization beyond the data you actually have.

And when you optimize against those estimates, your policy can discover places where the value function is wrong. It starts choosing actions because they look good to the critic, rather than because they actually lead to good outcomes. On-policy training gives you this very useful corrective loop: you try what your current policy wants to do, observe what happens, and update from that.

So I wouldn’t say off-policy data isn’t useful. It’s incredibly useful for learning representations, pretraining a policy, or learning a model of the world. But those are ways of extracting structure from the data without necessarily trusting it to tell you precisely how much better one action is than another under your current policy.

The tradeoff is efficiency versus stability. If fresh experience is cheap enough, it can be worth throwing away some statistical efficiency to get a learning process that’s harder to fool. In robotics, where collecting fresh experience is expensive, the pressure to make off-policy learning work is much stronger.
